name: Karim's
description: The century-old Mughlai institution in Gali Kababian, run by descendants of cooks who claim a lineage to the Mughal kitchens. Smoky seekh kebabs, mutton burra and a korma that has converted generations of Delhiites. Cramped, chaotic, unbeatable.
editor_note: Skip the butter chicken everywhere else and order the mutton burra with khameeri roti here instead.

name: Al Jawahar
description: Karim's quieter neighbour by Jama Masjid Gate No. 1, and many locals' actual pick of the two. The nihari at breakfast and the mutton korma are the moves, eaten under whirring fans with tandoor smoke drifting in from the front.
editor_note: Come before 10am for the nihari — it sells out, and that is not a marketing line.

name: Paranthe Wali Gali
description: A narrow Chandni Chowk lane where a handful of shops, some running since the 1870s, fry stuffed parathas in kadhais of ghee. Fillings run from classic aloo to rabri and papad, all served with the same set of sweet-and-sour chutneys.
editor_note: Pt. Gaya Prasad Shiv Charan is the one with the family tree on the wall — order the mixed plate and split it.

name: Natraj Dahi Bhalla Corner
description: A tiny 1940s counter near the Chandni Chowk metro that sells exactly two things: dahi bhalla and aloo tikki. Both arrive drowned in cold sweet curd and tamarind chutney, and both have queues that move with assembly-line speed.
editor_note: There is no seating and there never will be — eat standing in the lane like everyone has since 1940.

name: Old Famous Jalebi Wala
description: On the Dariba Kalan corner since 1884, frying thick, desi-ghee jalebis in enormous iron kadhais. These are not the wiry jalebis of sweet shops elsewhere — they are fat, syrup-heavy coils sold hot by the kilo.
editor_note: Ask for them taza, straight from the kadhai, and eat them walking into Dariba Kalan's silver lane.

name: Kuremal Mohan Lal Kulfi Wale
description: A Sitaram Bazar legend famous for stuffed-fruit kulfi — whole mangoes, pomegranates and oranges hollowed out, filled with kulfi and frozen. The fruit-cream flavours rotate with the season and taste like nothing made in a factory.
editor_note: Get the stuffed mango kulfi in summer and let them slice it like a fruit at the counter.

name: Jama Masjid at Sunrise
description: Shah Jahan's great mosque is at its best just after dawn, when the red sandstone courtyard is nearly empty and pigeons wheel over the minarets. Climb the southern minaret for a rooftop view of the old city waking up.
editor_note: Go at first light, before the tour groups, then walk straight to Al Jawahar for nihari.

name: Daryaganj Sunday Book Market (Mahila Haat)
description: The legendary Sunday second-hand book bazaar, now relocated into Mahila Haat but still the same sprawl of sellers with everything from pulp thrillers to out-of-print Penguin classics on tarpaulins. Books by the piece or, at some stalls, by the kilo.
editor_note: Carry cash, go before noon, and haggle gently — the good first editions vanish by lunchtime.

name: Khari Baoli Spice Market
description: Asia's largest wholesale spice market, running since the 17th century — sacks of dried chillies, nuts, pickles and teas stacked to the ceilings, with porters threading through clouds of pepper dust that will make you sneeze. Climb the stairs inside Gadodia Market for the rooftop view over Fatehpuri Masjid.
editor_note: The unmarked staircase in Gadodia Market leads to a rooftop panorama most visitors never find.

name: Kake Di Hatti
description: A 1942 dhaba near Fatehpuri Masjid serving naans the size of car tyres, stuffed with paneer, gobhi or keema-style soya, with dal makhani that simmers all day. Portions are built for sharing and the kitchen runs deep into the night.
editor_note: One stuffed naan feeds two people comfortably — order accordingly or be defeated.

name: Haji Mohd. Hussain Fried Chicken
description: Matia Mahal's answer to fried chicken everywhere else: birds marinated in a closely guarded masala and flash-fried in bubbling oil at the shopfront. Crisp, turmeric-stained and served with rumali roti and chutney on steel plates.
editor_note: Go after dark during Ramzan if you can — the whole lane turns into a festival around it.

name: Lala Babu Chaat Bhandar
description: A Chandni Chowk chaat counter where the kalmi vada and pao-style tikki have been drawing crowds for decades. Everything is assembled to order with a flick-of-the-wrist speed that is half the entertainment.
editor_note: The kalmi vada chaat is the sleeper hit — most first-timers wrongly default to the tikki.

name: Pandit Ved Prakash Lemon Wale
description: A century-old soda stall opposite Town Hall selling banta — lemon soda in marble-stoppered bottles — spiked with masala, kala namak and lime. The pop of the marble and the first salty-fizzy sip is pure Chandni Chowk summer.
editor_note: Order it kacha-nimbu style with extra masala and drink it fast before the fizz dies.

name: Giani's Di Hatti
description: The 1951 original near Fatehpuri Masjid that spawned the Giani's ice-cream chain, still best for what it started with: rabri faluda and hot gajar halwa in winter. The rabri is thick enough to fight your spoon.
editor_note: Winter rule of the old city: hot halwa first, faluda after, never the other way around.

name: Indian Coffee House
description: The worker-cooperative coffee house atop Mohan Singh Place, frozen somewhere in 1975 — turbaned waiters, sticky formica tables, filter coffee and mutton dosas for pocket change. Once the adda of journalists and revolutionaries; the terrace still catches the CP breeze.
editor_note: Order the cold coffee and a scrambled-egg toast, take the terrace seats, and stay all afternoon — nobody will hurry you.

name: Triveni Terrace Cafe
description: Tucked into the Triveni Kala Sangam arts complex near Mandi House, an open terrace cafe overlooking an amphitheatre and frangipani trees. Simple, honest thalis, keema pao and nimbu pani for the theatre-and-gallery crowd.
editor_note: Catch an exhibition downstairs, then get the mutton curry-chawal before the lunch rush of rehearsing actors arrives.

name: Oxford Bookstore
description: The grand old bookstore chain's Delhi flagship in Statesman House, with a serious India shelf, a children's corner and the Cha Bar attached — a tea menu running to over a hundred brews. Browsing here is an afternoon, not an errand.
editor_note: Buy your book, then claim a Cha Bar window seat with a pot of first-flush Darjeeling.

name: Agrasen ki Baoli
description: A 14th-century stepwell hidden between office towers off Hailey Road — 108 stone steps descending into cool, pigeon-haunted silence a minute from the CP roar. Equal parts architecture lesson and city escape hatch.
editor_note: Go at opening time on a weekday and you might have all 108 steps to yourself.

name: Wenger's
description: CP's Swiss-founded bakery, open since 1926 and still mobbed at all hours for shammi kebab patties, chicken croissants and rum balls handed over the marble counter. There is nowhere to sit; you eat on the colonnade like everyone else.
editor_note: The veg patties and a cold coffee from Depaul's two doors down is the classic CP loop.

name: Depaul's
description: A hole-in-the-wall on Janpath that has sold one perfect thing since 1956: cold coffee in a glass bottle, frothed sweet and strong. The bottle-return ritual at the counter is part of the institution.
editor_note: Ask for less sugar if you must, but drink it standing in the Janpath crowd — that is the format.

name: Kake Da Hotel
description: A gloriously unreformed Punjabi dhaba on the Outer Circle, slinging butter chicken, keema and dal over shared tables since 1931. The decor is strip lights and steel plates; the gravy makes up for everything.
editor_note: Share a table with strangers, order the butter chicken with tandoori roti, and don't ask for a menu card.

name: Saravana Bhavan
description: The Janpath outpost of the Chennai institution, with a queue on the pavement at most mealtimes. Ghee roast dosas, mini-tiffin platters and filter coffee poured from a height — reliable as a metronome.
editor_note: The queue moves faster than it looks; hold out for the mini tiffin so you get a bit of everything.

name: Cafe Lota
description: Inside the National Crafts Museum complex, a bamboo-shaded courtyard cafe that quietly rewrote what Indian cafe food could be — sabudana popcorn, palak patta chaat and millet bowls drawn from regional home kitchens. Pair it with the museum's textile galleries.
editor_note: Order whatever fish dish is on that week and finish with the dark chocolate-stuffed gulab jamun.

name: Kitty Su
description: The Lalit's flagship club and one of India's few genuinely inclusive dance floors, with drag nights, international techno and house bookings, and a crowd that actually dances. Multiple rooms mean you can flee the main floor when it peaks.
editor_note: Their drag and pride nights are the best parties in the city — book the guest list ahead.

name: 24/7 Restaurant at The Lalit
description: The Lalit's round-the-clock coffee shop, the classic Delhi answer to post-club hunger at 4am — biryani, ramen and club sandwiches served under chandeliers while the city sleeps. Pricey, but it is literally always open.
editor_note: The 4am biryani after a Kitty Su night is a Delhi rite of passage.

name: Unplugged Courtyard
description: A sprawling open-air bar in CP's Inner Circle built around a real tree strung with fairy lights, with acoustic acts most evenings. The food is dependable North Indian-meets-bar-bites; the draw is drinking under the open sky in the middle of CP.
editor_note: Reserve a courtyard table just before sunset and stay through the first live set.

name: The Big Chill Cafe
description: The movie-poster-plastered Khan Market institution that taught Delhi to love penne alfredo and mud pie in equal measure. Portions are enormous, the queue is eternal, and the dessert fridge has broken more diets than any place in town.
editor_note: Don't leave without the Mississippi mud pie, even if you have to take it to a Lodhi Garden bench.

name: Bahrisons Booksellers
description: Founded in 1953 by a refugee from Rawalpindi, this is Delhi's most loved bookshop — floor-to-ceiling shelves, staff who actually read, and a front-of-store table that sets the city's reading agenda. The kids' annexe nearby is just as good.
editor_note: Tell the staff the last book you loved and let them pick your next one — they're never wrong.

name: Khan Chacha
description: The kebab-roll counter that started in a Khan Market alley in 1972 and became shorthand for the rumali roll itself. Chicken tikka and mutton seekh wrapped with onion rings and chutney, eaten standing in the back lane.
editor_note: Mutton seekh roll, extra chutney, eaten in the middle lane while you window-shop — accept no substitutes.

name: Cafe Turtle
description: Perched above the Full Circle bookstore, a sunny top-floor cafe with mismatched colours, herbal teas, mezze platters and serious cakes. The kind of place where you climb up with a new book and lose two hours.
editor_note: Buy downstairs, read upstairs — and the banoffee pie with fresh mint tea is the house ritual.

name: Perch Wine & Coffee Bar
description: A pale, Scandinavian-quiet room doing double duty: precise pour-overs by day, a sharp wine list and small plates by night. The truffle croque and a glass of riesling is a complete Khan Market evening.
editor_note: Go at the 5pm changeover when the coffee crowd thins and the wine crowd hasn't arrived.

name: Gulati, Pandara Road
description: Anchor of the Pandara Road market, the strip of North Indian restaurants that has fed post-wedding and post-party Delhi since the 1960s. Butter chicken, dal Gulati and burra kebabs served fast, rich and unapologetic until well past midnight.
editor_note: Pandara Road at 1am, butter chicken with garlic naan, is the city's most reliable celebration.

name: Have More, Pandara Road
description: Gulati's eternal next-door rival, with partisans who will argue its dal makhani is the truer article. Same late hours, same gleaming gravies, slightly shorter queue — which is sometimes the whole decision.
editor_note: When Gulati's wait crosses thirty minutes, walk two doors down and lose nothing.

name: National Gallery of Modern Art
description: The country's flagship modern art museum in Jaipur House near India Gate — Amrita Sher-Gil, the Bengal School, Raza and Souza across echoing colonial halls and a sculpture garden. Quiet on weekdays to the point of feeling private.
editor_note: Head straight to the Amrita Sher-Gil rooms first, before the school groups land.

name: Summer House Cafe
description: The first-floor terrace bar above Aurobindo Place market that has hosted half of India's indie circuit on its tiny stage. Gig nights are sweaty and joyful; off nights it's a loose, fairy-lit terrace hang that runs late.
editor_note: Check their gig calendar — a weeknight show here beats most weekend clubbing in town.

name: Hauz Khas Social
description: The original Social, stacked down the side of Hauz Khas Village with windows over the lake and deer park. Laptops and cold brew by day, LIITs in jam jars and a roaring crowd by night — the village's most dependable constant.
editor_note: Come at 4pm for the lake-view window table and simply never leave.

name: The Toddy Shop
description: A Kerala kallu-shaap homage up a Hauz Khas Village staircase — beef fry, Kuttanadan duck, kappa and meen curry served on enamel plates under matinee posters of Malayalam cinema. Loud, homey and gloriously unfussy.
editor_note: Order the beef fry with Kerala parotta and thank whoever brought you here later.

name: Kunzum Travel Cafe
description: The pay-what-you-like travel cafe and bookshop that became a clubhouse for Delhi's wanderers — travel talks, photography walls, self-serve coffee and shelves of guidebooks and travelogues. More community room than commerce.
editor_note: Drop in for one chai, stay for the travel-stories evening, leave with three new trip plans.

name: auro kitchen & bar
description: A leafy Aurobindo Marg bungalow that flips from Mediterranean dinner garden to one of Delhi's best small electronic-music floors after dark. The booking policy keeps the dance floor crowd genuinely music-first.
editor_note: Their Sunday evening listening sessions in the garden are the gentlest way to end a weekend.

name: Deer Park
description: The wooded park stitched between Hauz Khas Village and Safdarjung Enclave, with spotted deer in their enclosure, peacocks at large, and running trails that link to the medieval lake. The village's green lung and decompression chamber.
editor_note: Enter from the village side at golden hour and loop the lake before dinner.

name: Hauz Khas Fort & Lake
description: Firoz Shah's 14th-century madrasa and tomb stepping down to the royal tank, now Delhi's favourite sunset ledge. Students, couples and sketchbook-carriers line the stone windows as parakeets cross the water.
editor_note: The arched windows on the lake side are the seats — claim one an hour before sunset.

name: Coast Cafe
description: A calm, white-walled room above the village bustle doing coastal South Indian properly — Malabar fish curry, appams, Coorg pandi curry and a quietly excellent cocktail list. The antidote to the street below.
editor_note: Appams with the stew arrive faster than your climb up three floors deserves.

name: Naivedyam
description: A dim, temple-dark South Indian stalwart at the mouth of Hauz Khas Village, serving rasam in steel tumblers as a free opener before crisp rava dosas and proper filter coffee. Unmoved by every trend that has swept the village around it.
editor_note: The complimentary rasam shot is the best thing you'll drink in the village — dosas are a bonus.

name: Potbelly Rooftop Cafe
description: A rooftop perch above Shahpur Jat's tangle, serving Bihari food that's nearly impossible to find elsewhere in Delhi — litti chokha, champaran mutton, sattu sharbat. The view over the urban village's terraces is half the charm.
editor_note: Litti chokha and a sattu cooler at sunset on this roof is the correct order of operations.

name: Flipside Cafe
description: A pocket-sized specialty coffee bar in a Shahpur Jat lane, all blond wood and a counter you can barely turn around at. Single-origin pour-overs, proper flat whites and bake-of-the-day; the baristas remember your order by visit two.
editor_note: It seats about eight people, so go odd hours and let the barista choose your beans.

name: Greenr Cafe
description: A plant-filled, plant-forward cafe that made vegetarian and vegan eating feel easy rather than earnest — smoothie bowls, jackfruit tacos, oat-milk everything. Laptop-friendly without being a co-working farm.
editor_note: The shiitake bao and a cold brew on the upstairs seats is the regulars' order.

name: Dada Jungi House Lane
description: Shahpur Jat's designer spine — a medieval-village lane where wedding ateliers, sneaker murals and indie studios share walls with buffalo sheds and old Jat havelis. Window-shopping here is an architecture-and-street-art crawl in one.
editor_note: Look up as much as you look in shop windows — the best murals are a floor above eye level.
